title: Your own types: classes and objects
summary: Bundle data with the functions that work on it, and create as many independent objects as you need.
license: Original work for Python Intelligence; license to be chosen by the owner
objective: Define classes whose objects keep their own state in attributes and change it through methods.
analogy: A class is a cookie cutter and each object is a cookie: same shape, but each cookie has its own icing.

misconceptions.belief: Attributes set in the class body belong to each object separately.
misconceptions.correction: A mutable class attribute is shared by every object; set per-object state in __init__ on self.

misconceptions.belief: `self` is a keyword Python fills in by magic.
misconceptions.correction: `self` is just the first parameter: Python passes the object the method was called on.

misconceptions.belief: Calling a method without parentheses runs it.
misconceptions.correction: `obj.method` is the method itself; `obj.method()` calls it.

rubric.evidence: each object keeps its own data, set up in __init__
operations on the data are methods that use self
methods return values (or change the object) as specified

review.recall: What does __init__ do, and why must a list attribute be created there rather than in the class body?

steps.title: Data and behaviour, together
steps.body:
A bank account has an owner and a balance, and you deposit into it. With what you know so far you'd keep
a dictionary for the data and separate functions for the actions, and hope they stay in sync. A
**class** puts the data and the actions in one place and lets you create as many accounts as you need.

steps.title: A blueprint and the things built from it
steps.body:
A class is a **blueprint**. Each object made from it (an **instance**) is a separate thing with its own
data, its **attributes**. The blueprint also describes what every instance can do: its **methods**,
which are functions that automatically receive the particular instance they were called on as their
first parameter, by convention named `self`.

questions: If two accounts are built from the same class, should depositing into one change the other?
In `acct.deposit(50)`, which object should `deposit` work on, and how does it know?

steps.title: Watch an object being built and changed
steps.body: Follow `self`: inside the methods it *is* the object `t`.

frames.note: The `class` block defines the blueprint `Tally` with two methods. Nothing runs yet.
`Tally(5)` creates a new, empty object and calls `__init__` on it.
`self` is the new object; `self.value = start` gives it an attribute.
`__init__` returns and the object is bound to `t`. Now call `t.tick()`.
`t.tick()` passes `t` as `self`, so the method changes `t` itself.
The change stayed with the object.

steps.title: The precise rules
steps.body:
```python
class Name:
    shared = 0                  # class attribute: one value shared by all instances

    def __init__(self, x):      # runs when Name(...) is called
        self.x = x              # instance attribute: one per object

    def method(self, y):        # obj.method(y) is Name.method(obj, y)
        return self.x + y
```

1. Calling the class, `obj = Name(5)`, creates an object and runs `__init__` with `self` bound to it.
2. `obj.method(a)` calls the method with `obj` as the first argument; you never pass `self` yourself.
3. Attributes set as `self.name = ...` belong to that one object. Forgetting `self.` makes a local
   variable that disappears when the method returns.
4. A class attribute is shared by every instance. Putting a **mutable** value there (such as a list)
   makes all instances share it; give each instance its own in `__init__` instead.
5. `__str__(self)` returns the text that `print(obj)` and `str(obj)` show.
6. Objects are mutable and names are labels, so `b = a` makes two names for the same object.

steps.title: Run it: two accounts
steps.body: Predict all four lines. Which one depends on two names sharing one object?
steps.code:
class Account:
    rate = 0.02

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance = self.balance + amount

    def __str__(self):
        return self.owner + ": " + str(self.balance)

a = Account("Ana", 100)
b = Account("Bo")
a.deposit(50)
print(a)
print(b)
print(a.rate, Account.rate)
alias = a
alias.deposit(1)
print(a.balance)

steps.title: Your turn: rectangles
steps.body:
Complete the class so `Rectangle(3, 4)` stores `width` and `height`, and has methods `area()` and
`perimeter()`.

tests.name: stores both sides
tests.code:
_r = Rectangle(3, 4)
assert (_r.width, _r.height) == (3, 4), 'store width and height as attributes on self'

tests.name: instances are independent
tests.code:
_a, _b = Rectangle(1, 2), Rectangle(5, 6)
assert _a.area() == 2 and _b.area() == 30, 'each rectangle keeps its own sides'

steps.title: Challenge: a stack that isn't shared
steps.body:
A stack is last-in, first-out. The starter `Stack` has `push`, `pop` and `is_empty`, and *seems* to work,
until you make two stacks. Fix it so every stack is independent, and make `pop` on an empty stack
raise `IndexError("pop from empty stack")`.
hints: `items = []` at class level is ONE list shared by every Stack. Where should each stack get its own?
Create `self.items = []` in an `__init__` method, and check `is_empty()` at the start of `pop`.

tests.name: last in, first out
tests.code:
_s = Stack()
_s.push(1)
_s.push(2)
assert _s.pop() == 2 and _s.pop() == 1 and _s.is_empty(), 'push 1, push 2: pop should give 2 then 1'

tests.name: stacks are independent
tests.code:
_a, _b = Stack(), Stack()
_a.push('x')
assert _b.is_empty(), 'pushing onto one stack must not change another: give each its own list in __init__'

tests.name: empty pop message

steps.title: Transfer: a scoreboard
steps.body:
Write a class `Scoreboard`. `add(player, points)` adds points to a player (starting from 0), `score(player)` returns a
player's total (0 for someone with no points), and `leader()` returns the player with the most points, ties going to
the name that comes first alphabetically, or `None` if nobody has scored. Two scoreboards must not share their scores.
hints: Create `self.scores = {}` in `__init__`, so each scoreboard gets its own dict.
For the leader: `min(self.scores, key=lambda p: (-self.scores[p], p))`, once you know the dict isn't empty.

tests.name: points add up per player
tests.code:
b = Scoreboard()
b.add('ana', 3)
b.add('ana', 4)
b.add('ben', 2)
assert (b.score('ana'), b.score('ben'), b.score('cy')) == (7, 2, 0)

tests.name: the leader, ties alphabetical
tests.code:
b = Scoreboard()
assert b.leader() is None
b.add('zed', 5)
b.add('amy', 5)
b.add('bob', 1)
assert b.leader() == 'amy', b.leader()

tests.name: the leader is the highest scorer, and changes
tests.code:
b = Scoreboard()
b.add('zed', 9)
b.add('amy', 2)
assert b.leader() == 'zed', b.leader()
b.add('amy', 10)
assert b.leader() == 'amy', b.leader()

tests.name: two scoreboards are separate
tests.code:
a, b = Scoreboard(), Scoreboard()
a.add('ana', 9)
assert b.score('ana') == 0 and b.leader() is None, 'the scoreboards share their scores: create them in __init__'

tests.name: Scoreboard is a class
tests.code: assert isinstance(Scoreboard, type) and isinstance(Scoreboard(), Scoreboard)

choices: Nothing; it must be passed explicitly
questions.explanation: Calling a method through an object passes that object as the first argument.
`n = n` only sets a local variable; nothing was stored on `self`, so the object has no attribute `n`.

questions.prompt: Without a `__str__` method, what does `print(obj)` show?
choices: A default description such as <__main__.Box object at 0x...>
questions.explanation: Python falls back to a generic description naming the class and the object's identity.

questions.prompt: Two instances both append to a list defined at class level. What happens?
choices: Both see all the appended items
Only the first instance can append
questions.explanation: A class attribute is shared by all instances; a mutable one is changed for everyone.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.body:
- Define a class with `__init__`, attributes on `self`, and methods.
- Create independent instances and call methods on them, knowing how `self` is passed.
- Give objects a readable `__str__`, and avoid shared mutable class attributes.

That completes the core Python path: you can now read, write and organise real programs.
